episodes.title: Episode 04: A correction, and a fresh start
notes: Correction: NEAT started from a broken copy of the pilot. Tanh output neurons squashed scores of 15 and 20 both to 1.0; ties picked the wrong action about 1 step in 9
Converted copy vs the real copy: boulder 30% vs 71%, wind 43% vs 92%
Fixed with identity outputs; the test now fails without the fix. Exact copy: ~98% wind, ~77% boulder (60 flights each)
Attempt D restarts with 2 route sensors, gentler mutation and 30% boulder flights mixed into the wind stages
Before the fix, the boulder stage reached 65% at best over 300 generations
transcript: This episode starts with a correction. In the first episode I told you that NEAT got a head start, a copy of the hand written pilot that landed about eighty two percent of the time. That copy was real. But the network NEAT actually received was not the same as that copy. It was a broken version of it. Let me explain how I found out, because it is a good story about checking your own work.

Here is where we were. The boulder stage had run for three hundred generations. With the boulder growing from small to full size, the best champion climbed from forty to sixty five percent landed. Real progress, but far too slow for ninety eight.

So I asked a simple question. The copy of the pilot, flown directly, how well does it handle the boulder? The answer was seventy one percent. But the same network, converted into NEAT's format at the very start, landed only thirty. In plain wind, ninety two against forty three. The same network should fly the same way. It didn't.

The cause was a single detail. NEAT's output neurons squash every value through a curve called tanh, which flattens out at one. The copied network gives each action a score, and some scores were as large as twenty. Squash twenty and you get one. Squash fifteen, and you also get one, exactly. So two actions were tied, and the computer picked the first one, not the best one. About one step in nine, the lander did the wrong thing. My test had missed it, because it used a small random network whose scores never got that large.

The fix was one line. The output neurons now pass their scores through unchanged. And I changed the test so that it fails without the fix and passes with it. The exact copy now lands about ninety eight percent of the time in full wind, and about seventy seven percent with the boulder. That's on small test sets, so take the numbers as rough. But it's a far better start than anything evolution reached after seven hundred generations from the broken one.

So I'm starting again. And since a restart was forced anyway, three more changes come with it. The network gets two more sensors, a kind of route guide. One says how far the lander is from where it should be heading, beside the boulder or over the pad. The other says how far it is above the boulder's top. Then, the mutations are gentler. I measured that small random changes to the weights cost about ten points with the boulder. That skill is fragile. And last, three in ten training flights in the wind stages now have a boulder in them. The network forgot skills twice when a stage didn't use them. This time selection keeps checking that skill all the way through.
To be clear about what still stands. The earlier stage results were real measurements. The runs really did pass calm air, the steady push and the gusts. They just did it from a handicapped start.

The new run began a few minutes ago, and the first generations land every calm flight. I'll tell you how far the exact copy plus evolution can get. And on the project page there is now a growing explanation of the network itself, what each part does, and how it changed as it evolved.

episodes.title: Episode 03: Gusts, a correction, and a missing skill
notes: Gusts stage passed at gen 202: 96% on 100 fresh flights, confirmed
Correction: the 92% full-wind check was selection luck; paired on 400 unseen flights it is 86.0% vs the pilot 91.0%
Found ahead of time: with the boulder the champion lands 14%, the cloned start network 25%, the pilot 77% (300 paired flights)
Change: the boulder stage now ramps the boulder size 40% → 100% (attempt C, same population, from gen 417)
transcript: Welcome back. Two hours ago the lander had just passed the steady push stage and beaten its teacher there. Since then it passed another stage, I had to correct a number, and I found a much bigger problem hiding further down the road.

First, the good news. The gusts stage passed. That's the real gusty wind, growing from weak to full strength, with turbulence still switched off. The champion landed ninety six out of a hundred fresh flights, and it held up on the confirmation. So the forgetting I told you about last time was repaired.

Then came turbulence, the twisting force, growing step by step to full strength. That's the complete wind task. And here's the correction. The best fresh check so far said ninety two percent landed. That sounded like a new record. But a check of a hundred flights, picked as the best of several, is flattering. That is the winner's curse again. So I flew that champion and the hand written pilot on the same four hundred unseen flights. The champion landed eighty six percent. The pilot landed ninety one. So in the full wind, evolution is still about five points behind its teacher. Turbulence is the hard part.

Now the bigger problem. I didn't want to wait for the boulder stage to find out how it would go. So I flew the current champion in the final world, with the boulder in the way. It landed only fourteen percent of the time. Then I went back to the very first network, the copy of the pilot that NEAT started from. Even that one landed only twenty five percent, while the pilot itself lands about seventy seven. So the copying worked for the wind, but it never really learned the boulder. The rules for the boulder are sharp. Steer to one side of it, and stay above it until you are past. A smooth network copying a pilot finds those sharp rules hard.

So the boulder has to be learned by evolution itself. And throwing a full size boulder at it right away would be like starting the wind at full strength. That's what the curriculum is for. So I made one change. In the boulder stage, the boulder now starts at forty percent of its size and grows to full size over about a hundred and fifty generations. I stopped the run, kept its whole population, and restarted it with that change. Nothing was lost. It carried on from generation four hundred and seventeen.

It is finishing the full wind stage now, and in about fifteen minutes it meets the first small boulders. That's the stage I expect to take longest. The deadline is next Wednesday evening, so there is time, but the boulder will decide whether ninety eight percent is reachable at all.
Next episode, when we see how evolution handles the rock.

episodes.title: Episode 02: Better than its teacher, and a lesson about forgetting
notes: Bug fixed: the steady push ignored its 5 → 15 ramp; training wheels turned down to 0.3 (full strength hurt the pilot)
Steady push passed at gen 76: 99% / 96% on two fresh sets of 100
Paired on 300 unseen flights, constant push 15: champion 97.3% vs pilot 82.3% (+15.0, 95% CI +10.7 to +19.3)
But in real gusts + turbulence: champion 64.3% vs pilot 92.3%. It specialised; the gusts stage must win it back
transcript: Welcome back. In the last episode, NEAT got its head start, a copy of a hand written pilot, and passed calm air in a few minutes. Since then, two things happened. One was a bug, and one was a surprise.

First, the bug. In the second stage, the lander faces a steady sideways push, like a constant wind from one side. The plan was to start the push gentle and make it stronger over the stage. But the push ignored that plan. It was always at full strength. On top of that, the training wheels were too firm. They are a gentle invisible hand that keeps the lander upright. I tested the hand written pilot with them. At full strength it landed a little less often than with no help at all, because the wheels stop the lander from tilting, and tilting is how it steers. With a light touch, about a third of the strength, it landed more often. So I stopped the first attempt, fixed the push, wrote a test for it, and turned the wheels down. Then I started again. Calm air passed immediately, in the very first generation.

Now the surprise. The steady push grew from gentle to full strength over about seventy generations. And then the champion passed the check. It landed ninety nine out of a hundred fresh flights, and ninety six on the confirmation. Then I compared it with its teacher, the hand written pilot, on the same three hundred unseen flights. Against a full strength steady push, the pilot landed about eighty two percent of the time. The evolved network landed about ninety seven percent. That is fifteen points better than the teacher, and the difference is clear, well outside the noise. For the first time in this project, evolution went past the pilot it started from.

But there is a catch, and it's an important one. I also flew the same champion in the real wind, the gusty kind, with turbulence. There it landed only sixty four percent of the time, while the pilot landed ninety two. So the network got very good at one kind of wind, and partly forgot the other. It specialised. That's a well known problem in curriculum learning, and now we have seen it here with real numbers.

Which is exactly why the next stage matters. It is running now. Real gusts, starting weak and growing to full strength, with turbulence switched off for the moment. The early generations look good, landing nearly every flight in gentle gusts. The question is whether it gets back to the pilot's level, and past it, once the gusts are at full strength. If it doesn't, the fix is clear. The steady push stage should be shorter, or mixed with real gusts, so the network never forgets them.

The run is doing about one generation every twenty five seconds. The gusts stage should reach full strength in roughly an hour. I'll check in every two hours, and the next episode comes when something passes or breaks.

episodes.title: Episode 01: A head start for NEAT
notes: Goal: ≥ 98% landed on 1,000 unseen flights in wind 15, turbulence 1.5 and a boulder, by Wed 4 Nov 18:00
Hand-written pilot, tuned with CMA-ES: 100% calm, 93.8% wind+turbulence, 74.2% with the boulder (500 unseen flights each)
NEAT starts from a 13-24-4 network cloned from the pilot with DAgger; its hidden neurons are protected
Six-stage curriculum; stage 1 (calm) passed at generation 5: 98% and 97% on two fresh sets of 100
transcript: Hello, and welcome to the first episode of the lander curriculum. You asked for something ambitious. A lunar lander that comes to rest between the flags ninety eight times out of a hundred, in strong gusty wind, with turbulence twisting it, and with a boulder floating in the way. The deadline is Wednesday evening. And you asked for NEAT, the method that evolves neural networks, but with a good starting network that has hidden layers.

Let me tell you why that matters. In the last wind project, plain NEAT started from tiny networks with no hidden neurons. And it kept them that way. It landed about ninety one percent of the time, and then it stalled. When I gave it a few hidden neurons, evolution simply deleted them.

So this time NEAT gets a head start. First, I wrote a pilot by hand. It leans into the wind using a drift sensor, a kind of home made accelerometer. It flies sideways to the pad before it descends, and it steers around the boulder. Then I let a second optimiser tune its gains. I tested the tuned pilot on five hundred flights it had never seen. In calm air it landed every single time. In wind and turbulence it landed about ninety four percent of the time. With the boulder added, seventy four percent. The boulder is clearly the hard part.

Next, I copied that pilot into a neural network with twenty four hidden neurons. The copying method is called DAgger. The network flies on its own, and at every moment the hand written pilot says what it would have done. So the copy also learns how to recover from its own mistakes. The copy lands about eighty two percent of the time across a mix of worlds. Not perfect, but a very good place to start.

Every network in NEAT's first population is a copy of that network, with a little noise. And this time the hidden neurons are protected. Evolution can tune them, and add more, but it can't delete them.

Then comes the curriculum. Six stages. Calm air first. Then a steady sideways push. Then real gusts, growing from weak to full strength. Then turbulence on top. Then the boulder. And finally a long polish with everything switched on. In the wind stages there are training wheels, a gentle invisible hand that keeps the lander upright, fading away over the stage. Every check is flown without it.

And the checks are strict. A stage only passes when the best network lands often enough on a hundred flights it has never seen, and then again on a second fresh hundred. The final goal will be measured on a thousand unseen flights.

The first stage is already done. In calm air, the champion landed ninety eight out of a hundred on the check, and ninety seven on the confirmation. That took just five generations, about three minutes. Now it is working on the steady push.

The honest caveat is this. Ninety eight percent is higher than anything I have measured in this task so far, even before the boulder. The hand written pilot gets about ninety four in wind alone. So we will see how far evolution can push past its teacher.
You can follow along on the project page, where every stage, check and new champion shows up in the log, with a replay of the lander at that moment. Next episode, when the wind gets real.
